title: #NoEstimates (Allen Holub)
summary: Allen Holub argues estimation is guesswork that breeds overtime and dysfunction, and that counting stories forecasts as well as story points.

assertions.quote: the main problem with estimates is that estimates are always based on guesswork you're always guessing
as soon as you have estimates you have deadlines and as soon as you have deadlines you have people working 18-hour days

verdicts.note: Deadline pressure is a documented driver of overtime, but the chain from estimate to crunch is not inevitable.

Time predictions change the work: software teams whose estimates were cut by up to 20% by clients were more productive, beyond 20% productivity fell, and estimates set 40% too low raised programmer error rates; overtime itself is not measured.

assertions.quote: if you've built the wrong program you have not succeeded in doing so much of value

verdicts.note: A framing about what counts as success rather than a measurable claim.

assertions.quote: what you ended up with was The Madness of taking story points and turning them into time

verdicts.note: Widely reported in practice surveys, but there is no measurement of how often it happens.

The book's description of the story-point method includes as a standard step converting points to work hours or capacity via measured productivity (velocity), so conversion to time is built into the method rather than a corruption of it.

assertions.quote: the only way you can make that number larger is to improve the environment

verdicts.note: Organizational friction does affect throughput, but velocity also varies with skill and task mix, so 'only' is too strong.

Enterprises over 5,000 employees are lower performers, attributed to heavyweight process and controls and tightly coupled architectures, and external change approval makes teams 2.6 times more likely to be low performers; this supports organisational constraints setting delivery throughput, though velocity and individual effort are not measured.

assertions.quote: we can just count stories and we get the same number either way

verdicts.note: Vasco Duarte's project data and some team analyses show story count tracks points closely, but this depends on stories being similarly sized.

Extrapolating measured progress from the first stage of work (the NoEstimates approach) is endorsed as a simple local model that few prediction models beat, but it is not compared head-to-head with story-point estimation.

assertions.quote: any backlog that's got a 100 stories on it has got something really wrong with it

verdicts.note: Requirements volatility is well documented; the claim that distant items are nearly worthless is plausible but unmeasured.

assertions.quote: if we're doing the wrong thing we have the option of fixing it here really early

verdicts.note: Incremental funding does reduce exposure, but cancelling early still needs some forecast of what remains.
